qt: to the Commission Letizia Moratti (PPE), Massimiliano Salini (PPE), Flavio Tosi (PPE), Salvatore De Meo (PPE), Giusi Princi (PPE), Marco Falcone (PPE), Caterina Chinnici (PPE), Fulvio Martusciello (PPE) Subject:

The Ceuta migrant crisis has brought a number of key issues to the fore, namely the management of irregular migrant flows, the security of Europe’s external borders and the functioning of the Schengen system. Press reports indicate that the Spanish Audiencia Nacional is verifying whether any people with links to jihadist terrorism – including extremists who are known to the authorities and individuals who have previously been deported for their radical inclinations – have crossed the border into Spain. The Ceuta migration crisis is clear proof that uncontrolled flows can facilitate the entry of people who pose a security risk. One cannot rule out the involvement of criminal networks or the possibility that external actors could be weaponising these migration flows. In this regard, any uncertainty or grey area in the management of migrant flows could cause issues not just for the two countries involved, but for Europe as a whole. As a result, Europe needs to test how effective the Entry/Exist system (which recently became fully operational) and the EU’s other border management tools are in emergency situations. In the light of the above: 1.

Does the Commission know whether any high-risk individuals have managed to enter the EU through Ceuta, and could it specify the nature of the checks that have been carried out by Europol, the SIS, Interpol and national authorities?

What measures will be taken to promptly step up border identification and screening procedures and bolster database interoperability with a view to preventing any breaches in the Schengen security architecture?

What urgent steps will be taken to introduce stricter conditions in the EU’s agreements with third countries with a view to supporting the Member States exposed to these migration flows and preventing the latter from being used as a geopolitical tool?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (11.11.2026) Information on possible infiltrations of persons posing a threat through Ceuta is collected and processed primarily by the competent Spanish authorities. The Commission continues to promote full use of the EU Entry/Exit System (EES), European Asylum Dactyloscopy Database Eurodac, Visa Information System, European Travel Information and Authorisation System and the interoperability framework set out in the relevant EU law1. Through funding and coordination with the European Union Agency for the Operational Management of Large-Scale IT Systems in the Area of Freedom, Security and Justice, the European Border and Coast Guard Agency and Member States, efforts focus on identification and screening of persons at external borders, including in crisis situations. The EES applies only to travellers crossing the official border crossing points, whereas persons who crossed illegally to Ceuta are expected to go through the screening procedure. Going forward as outlined in the 5-point plan to prevent, anticipate and respond to sudden, mass illegal arrivals2, the Commission intends to double down on efforts to prevent irregular migration by increasing cooperation with partners, strengthening EU external borders, improving monitoring, situational awareness and early warning systems, dismantling migrant smuggling and trafficking networks, and reinforcing returns and readmissions.
